transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. Could you start by telling me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Lee. Thank you for seeing me. Well, I suppose I'm here because... well, my daughter actually suggested I come in, because I just feel like I’m always, always up and moving. It’s the strangest thing. You know, I’m seventy years old, I’m retired now, I should be relaxing, but even on what is supposed to be a completely quiet day at home, I just can't seem to settle down. 

I’ll tell myself I’m just going to sit in my favorite chair and rest, but then I’m up, bouncing over to the kitchen counter to look at the garden club list. I help organize the spring luncheon, you see, which is quite an ordeal with everyone's dietary needs these days, making sure everyone is bringing the right dish. But before I even finish sorting that out or writing anything down, I’m wandering over to my knitting bag in the living room. I'm making a little yellow blanket for my grandniece. But I don't stay there either! I'll do maybe two stitches, and the next thing I know, I'm digging through the desk in the den for my travel papers for this little bus trip I'm taking next month. 

It’s just... I go from the garden club list, to the knitting bag, to the travel papers, just bouncing around the house all day long. And before I’ve really finished any one thing, the day is entirely over. I just never stop moving, and frankly, it's getting a bit exhausting to feel like I have this motor inside me that just won't switch off so I can enjoy a peaceful afternoon.
Over this same period, have you noticed that you need less sleep than usual to feel rested, or are you sleeping a normal amount?

Oh, goodness no, I definitely still need my sleep. It's not like I can just run on two hours and feel fine, no, no. If anything, by the time I finally get into bed after all that bouncing around the house I was just telling you about, I am completely worn out. 

I usually try to get to bed around 10:30... well, sometimes it's closer to 11:00 if I get caught up watching one of those British mystery programs on PBS. They always draw me in right at the end, you know how they do, and you just have to know who did it. But I always make sure I get my full eight hours, or at least seven and a half. My daughter actually bought me this wonderful mattress topper last Christmas—memory foam, I think it's called—and it's just lovely. 

Once I'm in bed, I really do sleep a completely normal amount. I mean, I might get up once in the night to use the restroom, which is just part of being seventy, I suppose, but I certainly don't feel like I can just skip my rest. If I don't get a proper night's sleep, I absolutely feel it the next morning. I'm not one of those people who can just close their eyes for a few hours and spring out of bed ready to take on the world. I need my rest! It's just that once the sun is up and I've had my coffee, well, I'm off to the races again. So, yes, my sleep is quite normal, I definitely still need it.
Have you noticed any unexplained weight loss, feeling unusually hot or sweaty, a racing heart, or shakiness in your hands during this time?

Oh, no, no, nothing like that. Goodness, weight loss? I wish! No, my weight has stayed exactly the same for the last, oh, it must be fifteen years now. Ever since I retired from the school cafeteria, actually. I used to be on my feet all day there, serving the children, but even now with all my bouncing around the house that I was telling you about, the scale hasn't budged a single pound. I suppose my body is just used to being at this weight. 

And as for feeling hot or sweaty, well, it's quite the opposite, really! I'm usually the one putting on a sweater. I have this lovely blue wool cardigan that I keep draped over the back of the sofa, because even in the summer, if the air conditioning is on even a little bit, I get a terrible chill. My daughter always tells me I keep the house too warm when she comes over to visit, but I just don't like the cold at all. So no, definitely not unusually hot or anything like that. 

And my heart... well, it just beats along at its normal pace, as far as I can tell. I don't feel it fluttering or racing or doing anything out of the ordinary, even when I'm scurrying from room to room. And my hands are perfectly steady! Which is a blessing, really, because if my hands were shaking, I wouldn't be able to do my knitting. You know, I was mentioning that yellow blanket for my grandniece earlier—well, you need a very steady hand for the purl stitches, especially with the finer yarn I'm using for it. It's a very delicate baby yarn, so soft, but if your hands shake even a little bit, you drop a stitch and then you have to unravel the whole row, which is just so frustrating. I simply wouldn't have the patience for it. So, thank heavens, my hands are perfectly fine. It's really just this restless energy making me pace about, but no shaking or sweating or anything like that.
Along with this constant urge to move from task to task, do you also find yourself worrying excessively about things—like your health, family, or finances—more days than not?

Oh, goodness, no. I wouldn't say I'm a worrier. I mean, everyone worries a little bit, don't they? If you watch the evening news for more than five minutes, you'd think the sky was falling. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she watches those 24-hour news channels all day long, and she's just a bundle of nerves about everything—the economy, the weather, you name it. But me? No, I really don't let those things get to me. 

As for my health, well, I feel quite blessed, honestly. Other than this... this inability to just sit still and read a book or watch a program without popping up every two minutes, I feel fine. I go to my primary care doctor, Dr. Evans—he's been my doctor for, oh, twenty years now, since his clinic was over on Elm Street before they moved to that big new medical center—and he always says my numbers are wonderful for my age. Blood pressure is good, cholesterol is fine. So I don't sit around fretting about my health, no.

And my family, well, my daughter is doing just beautifully. She's a regional manager for a bank, very responsible, very sensible. She's the one who suggested I come see you, actually, because she noticed how I was just buzzing around the house like a trapped bee when she came over for Sunday dinner. But I don't worry about her. She's got her head on straight. And finances... well, like I said, I'm retired, I have my pension from the school district, and my late husband, Arthur, he set up a very nice little annuity for me before he passed. It's not a fortune, but it pays the bills and lets me take my little bus trips and buy nice yarn for my knitting. 

So, no, I don't have this dark cloud of worry hanging over me. I'm not lying awake at night agonizing over bills or health scares. It's really just the opposite—I'm almost too energetic, too eager to get to the next thing, even when I don't know what the next thing is! It's the physical restlessness, the bouncing from the garden club list to the knitting to the travel papers, that's what's bothering me. But in my mind? No, I'm quite content, not worried at all.

Thinking back to when you were a child or a young adult, did you tend to be a restless, fidgety, or easily distracted person back then, or is this constant need to move from task to task something that's really only shown up more recently?

Oh, goodness, no, it's certainly not a new thing at all. If I really sit and think about it—and my daughter and I were actually just talking about this very thing the other day when she came over—I’ve been this way for as long as I can remember. 

Even way back in grade school, oh, it must have been the late nineteen-fifties, I remember my teachers always having the same things to say about me. I had Mrs. Higgins for third grade, a lovely woman with these very thick spectacles, and she used to pull my mother aside at parent-teacher night. She'd tell her, and I remember my mother repeating this to my father at the dinner table, she'd say that I was a very bright girl, but I was just so scattered. That was the word they always used, scattered. 

And she was right, I really was! I was always losing my papers. I’d do my spelling words or my arithmetic homework, and I'd just shove the paper in my desk or my bookbag, and then poof, it was gone when it was time to turn it in. My mother was always having to help me dig through my things. And I just could not keep quiet, either. I was always talking out of turn, just blurting things out before Mrs. Higgins even finished asking the question, because the thought would pop into my head and I just had to get it out right that second. 

And the wiggling! Oh my, I was always wiggling in my seat. I just couldn't sit still long enough to finish my work. I’d get halfway through a reading assignment and suddenly I just had to adjust my skirt, or tap my Mary Janes on the floor, or turn around to see what the boy in the desk behind me was doing. My mother used to say I had ants in my pants, bless her heart. She tried her best to get me to settle down and focus, but it was just how I was wired, I suppose. So, yes, this whole business of bouncing around and not being able to just sit and focus... it's definitely not some new thing that just popped up since I retired. It’s been my constant companion since I was a little girl with pigtails!
